title: The Alpine Premium: Trentino-Alto Adige Pays Nearly Five Cents Over Italy at the Pump
dek: Self-service Benzina in the mountain region ran €2.0495 on August 7th against a national €2.0026 — yet prices there have been falling three days straight.
body: Self-service motorists in Trentino-Alto Adige paid €2.0495 for Benzina and €2.1504 for Gasolio on August 7th, putting the region 4.69 cents above the national self-service petrol average of €2.0026 and 3.65 cents above the national diesel figure of €2.1139. The premium is not uniform across the forecourt, though: full-service diesel actually comes in cheaper here than nationally, €2.2632 against €2.2681. The real outlier is Metano, listed at €1.7993 self-service versus €1.5610 nationally — a gap of nearly 24 cents, and a reminder that in a region of 392 stations a thin compressed-gas sample carries a lot of weight in the average.

Direction matters as much as level, and here it points down. Self-service Benzina has slipped for three consecutive days from its August 4th peak of €2.0562, shedding 0.67 cents, while Gasolio has come off €2.1593 to €2.1504 over the same stretch — a 0.89-cent decline, with half a cent of it arriving in the last twenty-four hours alone. Full-service Metano has moved the opposite way, climbing four days running from €1.6322 to €1.6776. Behind all of it sits an unusually diligent network: 392 stations registered in the region and 372 of them filing prices, a 94.9% reporting rate that comfortably beats the 90.7% recorded nationally (21,733 of 23,959). The registered count has also crept up from 390 to 392 across the tracked window — small numbers, but a network that is being kept current rather than left to drift.

Reading a market at this resolution — one region a day, four fuels, self and full service, each with its own running history — is precisely the kind of work a hand-maintained spreadsheet cannot survive. Fuel Dashboard sidesteps that by rebuilding itself every morning: it ingests the MIMIT open data, recomputes the national, regional, provincial and municipal aggregates, regenerates the charts and republishes the site with nobody opening a file. The entire pipeline was built with Claude Code, and the dividend is that the daily effort goes into interpreting the numbers instead of assembling them.
pull_quote: Trentino-Alto Adige runs Italy's most diligent reporting network — 372 of 392 stations filed prices — and still charges 4.7 cents over the national petrol average.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight falls on Trentino-Alto Adige, and it carries a clear alpine premium: self-service Benzina at €2.0495 against a national average of €2.0026, nearly five cents more. Diesel tells the same story on a smaller scale, €2.1504 regionally versus €2.1139 nationally.

But the trend is heading the other way. Self-service petrol in the region has now fallen three days in a row, down 0.67 cents from its August 4th peak, with diesel off 0.89 cents over the same stretch. Metano is the eye-catcher on the other side of the ledger: €1.7993 self-service against €1.5610 nationally, a gap of almost 24 cents. And the region reports better than anywhere the national average would suggest — 372 of 392 registered stations filed prices today, a 94.9% reporting rate versus 90.7% across Italy.

All of this comes from Fuel Dashboard, a project tracking Italian fuel prices daily from MIMIT open data: national and regional averages across Benzina, Gasolio, GPL and Metano, self and full service, with day-by-day history and a different region in the spotlight every morning. Have a look: https://adeo-blip.github.io/fuel-price-italy/

The project is really an argument about method. Maintained by hand in Excel, a dashboard like this lasts about two weeks — download the CSV, clean it, recompute the averages, re-export the charts, then do it all again tomorrow. Instead the whole pipeline runs itself each morning: ingest, aggregate, regenerate, republish. I built it with Claude Code, and that is the honest case for AI coding tools — not typing code faster, but making a project sustainable that otherwise would never have been worth starting.
